Name: Buddhism (Theravada)
Description: The oldest surviving branch of Buddhism, emphasizing individual enlightenment through the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
CreationMyth: Buddhist cosmology describes cycles of creation and destruction (kalpas) rather than a single creation event. The universe arises from collective karma.
CorePrinciples: Four Noble Truths: Life involves suffering, suffering arises from craving, suffering can cease, the path to cessation is the Eightfold Path
Anatta (no-self): There is no permanent, unchanging self
Anicca (impermanence): All conditioned things are impermanent
Karma: Actions have consequences across lifetimes
Nirvana: Liberation from the cycle of rebirth

Name: Christianity (Catholic)
Description: The largest Christian denomination, emphasizing apostolic succession, sacraments, and the authority of the Pope.
CreationMyth: God created the universe in six days and rested on the seventh. Humans were created in God's image, fell from grace through original sin, and await redemption.
CorePrinciples: Trinity: One God in three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit)
Salvation through Jesus Christ's death and resurrection
Seven Sacraments as means of grace
Papal infallibility in matters of faith and morals
Natural law and moral theology
Social justice and preferential option for the poor

Name: Islam (Sunni)
Description: The largest denomination of Islam, following the Sunnah (practices) of Muhammad and the first four caliphs.
Sources: Four schools of jurisprudence (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali)
CreationMyth: Allah created the heavens and earth in six days. Adam was created from clay, and all humans descend from Adam and Eve.
CorePrinciples: Tawhid: Absolute monotheism - Allah is one and indivisible
Five Pillars: Shahada (faith), Salat (prayer), Zakat (charity), Sawm (fasting), Hajj (pilgrimage)
Prophets: Muhammad is the final prophet in a line including Abraham, Moses, and Jesus
Quran is the literal word of God
Sharia: Divine law governing all aspects of life
Ummah: Universal Muslim community

Name: Hinduism (Advaita Vedanta)
Era: 8th century CE - Present (philosophy); roots in 1500 BCE (Vedas)
Description: Non-dualistic school of Hindu philosophy teaching that Brahman (ultimate reality) and Atman (individual soul) are identical.
CreationMyth: Creation is cyclical, emerging from Brahman through Maya (cosmic illusion). The universe undergoes endless cycles of creation and dissolution.
CorePrinciples: Brahman: Ultimate, unchanging reality
Maya: The illusory nature of the material world
Atman = Brahman: Individual consciousness is identical to universal consciousness
Moksha: Liberation through realization of one's true nature
Karma and reincarnation
Jnana Yoga: Path of knowledge and self-inquiry

Name: Taoism
Description: Chinese philosophical and religious tradition emphasizing living in harmony with the Tao (the Way).
CreationMyth: The Tao is the source of all existence. From the Tao came the One, from the One came Yin and Yang, from these came all things.
CorePrinciples: Tao: The fundamental nature of the universe
Wu wei: Non-action or effortless action in harmony with natural flow
Yin and Yang: Complementary opposites in dynamic balance
Simplicity and naturalness
Non-attachment to outcomes
Three Treasures: compassion, frugality, humility

Name: Judaism (Orthodox)
Description: Traditional form of Judaism adhering strictly to Torah law and rabbinic interpretations.
CreationMyth: God created the world in six days. Humans are created in God's image and given dominion over the earth. Jews are God's chosen people with whom He made a covenant.
CorePrinciples: Monotheism: One God, creator of the universe
Torah as divine revelation
613 Mitzvot (commandments)
Covenant between God and the Jewish people
Messiah will come to redeem Israel
Importance of study, prayer, and observance
Tikkun Olam: Repairing the world

Name: Confucianism
Description: Chinese ethical and philosophical system emphasizing moral cultivation, social harmony, and proper conduct.
CorePrinciples: Ren (仁): Humaneness, benevolence
Li (禮): Ritual propriety, proper conduct
Filial piety: Respect for parents and ancestors
Five Relationships: ruler-subject, father-son, husband-wife, elder-younger, friend-friend
Junzi: The ideal of the cultivated person
Education and self-cultivation
Meritocracy in governance

Name: Stoicism
Description: Ancient Greek philosophy teaching that virtue, reason, and living in accordance with nature lead to eudaimonia (flourishing).
CorePrinciples: Dichotomy of control: Focus only on what you can control
Virtue is the sole good; vice is the sole evil
Living according to nature and reason
Apatheia: Freedom from destructive emotions
Amor fati: Love of one's fate
Cosmopolitanism: All humans are part of one universal community
Memento mori: Remember death

Name: Secular Humanism
Description: Non-religious philosophy affirming human dignity, reason, ethics, and justice without supernatural beliefs.
CorePrinciples: No supernatural or divine authority
Human reason and science as tools for understanding
Ethical values derived from human experience and empathy
Individual autonomy and freedom of thought
Democratic values and human rights
Social responsibility and altruism
Critical thinking and skepticism

Name: Indigenous Australian Dreamtime
Description: Aboriginal Australian spiritual framework where ancestral beings created the land and established law and culture.
CreationMyth: During the Dreamtime, ancestral spirits rose from the earth and sky, creating the land, animals, plants, and people. These beings established the laws and customs before transforming into features of the landscape.
CorePrinciples: All life is interconnected
Land is sacred and holds ancestral presence
Custodianship rather than ownership of land
Circular time: past, present, and future coexist
Knowledge transmitted through story, song, and ceremony
Kinship systems define social responsibilities
Balance and harmony with nature
